name: Rambutan
summary: This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant a grafted rambutan of a good variety and care for it until the first fruits. It is for backyards and small orchards in warm, humid places.
season: Grafted seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July, so they settle in with steady rain. Rambutan likes a warm, humid place with rain spread through much of the year.
material: A grafted seedling of a proven variety, such as R5, R162, Rongrien or another sweet, red fruited selection, joined to a seedling rootstock. Rootstocks are grown from fresh seed for about 8 to 12 months, grafted, and planted out about 6 months after grafting. Trees from seed take longer to bear and give mixed fruit, and many seedlings turn out to be male trees with few or no fruits.
spacing: About 8 to 10 m between trees and between rows, one grafted seedling a hole. Holes about 30 cm wide and deep, wider on hard soil.
water: Mostly rain fed. New trees are shaded and watered in dry spells, and the base is kept mulched. Growers with water on hand irrigate in long dry months so the trees flower and fruit well.
fertilizer: Compost or dried manure in the hole. About 60 g of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) around a young tree at first, then about 200 g a tree in the second year, 300 g in the third and 400 g in the fourth, split between the start and the end of the rains. Bearing trees get more, with potash for sweet fruit.
care: Shading new trees for the first weeks, ring weeding every three months, mulching, removing rootstock shoots, shaping to a low, open tree, and cutting and burning twigs hit by borers. Checking new shoots and fruits for mealybugs and fruit borers.
harvest: Fruit is ready when the skin turns pinkish red to red, and the fruits in one bunch ripen at different times, so growers pick in rounds, often three times a week at the peak. Bunches are cut with shears or a hooked pole, kept in the shade, sorted by size and ripeness and packed in boxes with air holes.

ways.label: Grafted seedling (grafted na rambutan)

steps.title: Clear the land and mark the spots
steps.how: Clear the brush and stumps and loosen the soil. Mark the planting spots about 8 to 10 m apart each way, since rambutan grows into a wide tree.

steps.title: Dig the holes
steps.how: Dig holes at least 30 cm wide and 30 cm deep, wider than the seedling bag on hard soil. Mix the topsoil with compost or dried manure for filling back.

steps.title: Plant the grafted seedling
steps.how: Remove the bag without breaking the soil ball and set the seedling in the hole with the graft above the soil. Fill in with topsoil, press it gently and water well.

steps.title: Shade the new tree
steps.how: Shade the new tree with fronds or a net for its first weeks, and longer if the weather is hot and dry, so it recovers from planting. Water it in dry spells and mulch around the base.

steps.title: First fertilizer
steps.how: Put about 60 g, or 6 tablespoons, of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) around the base and cover it lightly with soil. Repeat a few times a year, a little more as the tree grows.

steps.title: Ring weed every three months
steps.how: Weed a circle around each tree every three months or whenever the grass grows back. Lay the cut grass as mulch a little off the stem.

steps.title: Remove rootstock shoots
steps.how: Rub off any shoot that comes from below the graft. Keep the good variety growing as the main stem.

steps.title: Watch for twig borers and mealybugs
steps.how: Look for twigs that wilt or have small holes, and for white mealybugs on new shoots. Cut and burn damaged twigs.

steps.title: Feed more in the second year
steps.how: From the second year, give about 200 g of complete fertilizer a tree, about 300 g in the third year and about 400 g in the fourth. Split each year's amount between the start and the end of the rains.

steps.title: Shape the young tree
steps.how: Keep a few strong, well spread main branches and cut out weak, crossing or low branches. A low, open tree is easier to pick and to protect.

steps.title: First fruits
steps.how: Pick when the skin turns pinkish red or fully red, going over the tree in rounds since the fruits ripen unevenly. Cut the bunches with shears or a pole hook without breaking the branches, which bear the next crop.

ways.note: Rambutan usually starts bearing at about 4 to 5 years.

mistakes: Planting seedlings from seed, which may turn out to be male trees with few fruits.
Planting in full sun with no shade in the first weeks.
Tearing branches when picking, which costs the next crop.
Picking whole bunches at once while many fruits are still green.
Leaving twig borer damage on the tree.
better: Plant grafted seedlings of a proven variety from an accredited nursery.
Test the soil and feed by the result, raising the amount each year.
Water during long dry spells so flowering and fruit set stay even.
Prune lightly after each harvest to keep the tree low and open.
Scout for twig borers, fruit borers and mealybugs every month and clean up fallen fruit.
Pick in rounds with shears and sort the fruit for a better price.

watering.traditional: Rambutan here is mostly rain fed: a new tree is shaded, mulched and watered in dry spells, and grown trees live on the rain. Growers with a creek or a pump water bearing trees in long dry months so they flower and fill their fruit well.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a mulched ring for young trees. Basin, small sprinklers or drip under bearing trees where water is near. Water in the cool early morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin, shade the new tree, and keep a thick mulch of cut grass a little off the stem. Rambutan fits places with rain through most of the year. Where the dry season is long, rain fed trees bear lightly and young trees need water carried to them.
watering.dryseason: Young trees about twice a week. Bearing trees every 5 to 7 days from the first flowers until picking, after a short dry rest before flowering. Water when the young leaves droop and curl by midday.
watering.wet: Rambutan wants moist but well drained soil. Waterlogged trees yellow and their roots rot. Plant on sloping or raised ground, drain flat spots, and keep water away from the trunk. Long rain at flowering spoils pollination and brings fruit rot.

schedule.often: Soak at planting, then every 2 to 3 days when no rain falls, under shade
schedule.amount: A good soak of a ring basin around the stem
schedule.why: The young graft has a small root ball and wilts fast in sun and dry soil.

schedule.often: About twice a week in the dry months, once a week on heavy soil
schedule.amount: A soak of the mulched ring under the leaves
schedule.why: Rambutan is touchy about drought, and young trees stall or die in a dry month.

schedule.often: About once a week in the dry months where water is near
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring, widened as the crown spreads
schedule.why: Steady leaf flushes build the crown that will carry fruit.

schedule.stage: Bearing trees: short dry rest before flowering (each year)
schedule.often: Hold back water for a few weeks at the end of the rains or in the dry months, until the leaves stop flushing
schedule.amount: None, or a light watering only if leaves wilt badly
schedule.why: Drier soil stops new leaves and lets the tree flower.

schedule.often: Once the flower panicles show, water every 5 to 7 days in dry weather
schedule.amount: A deep soak of all the ground under the crown
schedule.why: Dry soil now drops flowers and newly set fruits.

schedule.often: Every 5 to 7 days in dry weather, keeping moisture even
schedule.amount: A deep soak under the crown. A big bearing tree drinks far more now than at any other time
schedule.why: Fruits that go thirsty stay small, with thin flesh, and may split.

schedule.often: Water with the after harvest feeding and pruning if the rains have not come
schedule.amount: A deep soak under the crown
schedule.why: Two good leaf flushes after harvest feed next year's flowers.

critical: The first two years, since young rambutan does not stand drought.
Flowering and fruit set, when dry soil sheds flowers and small fruits.
Fruit growth, when a dry spell gives small fruits with thin flesh.

signs.dry: Young leaves droop and curl, leaf tips and edges brown, flowers and small fruits fall, and fruits stay small with thin flesh.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves, rotting roots and slow decline on waterlogged ground, and more rotting fruits in long rains.

better: Water steadily from flowering to harvest with drip or under tree sprinklers, after a short dry rest. This gives better fruit set and bigger fruits than rain alone.
Keep the mulch thick and shade young trees in their first months, the cheapest way to get them through the dry season.
